title: my first PCB design
body:
This was my first complete PCB design project. I followed the hardware design process for an STM32WB Bluetooth Low Energy board and used KiCad to go from a blank project to a board that could eventually be sent to a manufacturer. I followed the [tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nkHFoxe0mrU) on this PCB by Phil's Lab, going over two parts of the 3-part tutorial.

I learned a lot from this project, and it was my first time working towards creating a fully functioning PCB from the ground up. Each step in the PCB design process was challenging, brought up circuit fundamentals, and introduced new aspects of design to keep in mind. This took me 3 weeks, or about 5 days of work, to accomplish. 

## 1. Documentation

Before working on the schematic, I went over the MCU (microcontroller unit) [datasheet](https://www.st.com/en/microcontrollers-microprocessors/stm32wb55ce.html) for the STM32WBCE, including application notes and reference designs, to properly implement the unit.

I used the MCU datasheet, ST application notes, reference schematics, and component datasheets to understand things such as:

- which pins needed power
- which pins needed decoupling capacitors
- how the internal power supply circuitry worked
- what crystals were required
- how to connect the Bluetooth RF output
- what external components were recommended

For example, the STM32WB has several power pins and power domains rather than one simple power input. The design tied the required supplies to 3.3 V and placed local capacitors around the MCU according to the intended power connections.

## 2. Schematic

![](/images/uploads/image-5.png)

The schematic was where the electrical design was created before worrying about the physical PCB.

I started with the STM32WB MCU and added the supporting circuitry around it. This included the power system, clocking, USB, programming/debug connections, and Bluetooth RF section.

### 2.1 Main Components

The **STM32WB microcontroller** is the main device on the board. It runs the firmware and contains the Bluetooth Low Energy functionality.

The **voltage regulator** takes the 5 V coming from USB and converts it into 3.3 V for the MCU and other circuitry.

The **crystals** provide accurate timing references for the MCU and need to be placed close to the oscillator pins.

The **RF matching network and filter** prepare the Bluetooth signal before it reaches the antenna connector.

The **USB connector** provides both power and USB communication, while the **ESD protection device** helps protect the interface from electrostatic discharge.

The **SWD/debug connection** is used for programming and debugging, while the **UART connection** provides another communication interface during development.

### 2.2 Decoupling Capacitors

A small capacitor is placed next to the MCU power pin to provide a stable current to the overall circuit. As the power source does not provide DC all the time, the capacitors are there to maintain the current. Therefore, smaller capacitors are placed next to the MCU. A larger capacitor was also used as bulk decoupling for the MCU.

The PCB placement matters just as much as having the capacitor in the schematic. The capacitors should be physically close to the corresponding power and ground pins(vias) so the current path stays short and low-inductance.

# 3. PCB

![](/images/uploads/image-6.png)

### 3.1 PCB Component Placement

Depending on the importance of ____, we place certain components closer to ____.

### 3.2 The Four Layers

Usually, more complex PCB designs require more than 40 layers, as this allows more components to fit within a smaller area and at a greater thickness. 

![image.png](/images/uploads/image-10.png)

Our board uses four copper layers. 

**Layer 1 — F.Cu (components)**

The top layer contains all of the components and important signal routing.

This includes connections around the MCU as well as signals such as USB and RF.

**Layer 2, 3 — In1.Cu, ln2.Cu (GND)**

The two internal layers are **ground planes**.

Current travels down traces and returns to its source.

For high-frequency signals, the return current prefers to flow through the nearby ground plane underneath the signal trace.

That means a top-layer trace and the ground plane underneath it work together.

This is especially important for RF and other fast signals.

Keeping the ground plane continuous gives the return current a short path and helps reduce noise and unwanted electromagnetic interference.

**Layer 4 — B.Cu (3.3V distribution)**

The bottom layer is used for additional routing and a large **3.3 V copper pour**.

Vias assigned to the 3.3 V net connect into this copper area, allowing power to be distributed around the PCB without routing a separate long trace to every device.

### 3.3 Vias

Vias are plated holes that electrically connect copper between PCB layers.

For example:

**3.3 V copper → via → capacitor → MCU power pin**

A ground connection can similarly go:

**component ground → ground via → internal ground plane**

Many decoupling capacitors have both a **3.3 V via and a GND via** to**** keep current connections shorter.

### 3.4 Stitching Vias



### 3.5 Powering the Board

The board receives power through USB.

The basic power path is:

**USB 5 V → voltage regulator → 3.3 V → MCU and other circuitry**

The voltage regulator is placed close to the USB power entry point, with input and output capacitors nearby.

The 3.3 V supply is then distributed through copper pours, traces, and vias around the PCB.

Trace width depends on what the trace is doing.

Power and ground connections are generally wider because wider copper has lower resistance and lower inductance.

A useful rule I learned was:

**short + wide = better for power and ground**

This is especially important around the voltage regulator, MCU power pins, and decoupling capacitors.

Normal low-speed digital signals can use smaller traces because they carry relatively little current.

### 3.6 Fiducial Markers

The three small circular features near the edges of the PCB are **fiducial markers**.

They are not electrical components. Automated assembly machines use cameras to locate these markers and determine the exact position and rotation of the PCB before placing components.

### 3.7 Mounting Holes

The four larger holes are **mounting holes**.

They are mechanical features used to attach the PCB to an enclosure, standoffs, or another structure.

They need enough clearance from traces, components, and the board edge.

## 4. Traces and Routing

Routing was where I started understanding that PCB traces are not all treated the same.

The more critical connections were routed first, followed by lower-speed and less sensitive signals.

### 4.1 Routing Priority

The most important sections were routed first, including:

- Bluetooth RF
- power circuitry
- USB differential pair
- crystal connections

Lower-speed signals such as GPIO, UART, reset, and LED connections are more forgiving and can be routed afterward.

Routing critical signals first allows them to take the shortest and cleanest paths before the board becomes crowded.

### 4.2 Routing Between Layers

Sometimes there was not enough room to route a signal directly across the top layer.

In these cases, the signal could go:

**[F.Cu](http://F.Cu) → via → [B.Cu](http://B.Cu) → via → [F.Cu](http://F.Cu)**

The first via takes the signal down to the bottom layer, the trace travels underneath the crowded area, and another via brings the signal back up.

This helped me understand that PCB routing happens in three dimensions rather than only across a flat surface.

### 4.3 Bluetooth RF Routing

The Bluetooth RF section introduced me to controlled-impedance routing.

The STM32WB RF output cannot simply be connected to the antenna using any random trace.

The design uses an impedance-matching network and RF filter before reaching the antenna connector.

The RF trace is designed around a **50 Ω characteristic impedance**.

Its width depends on the PCB stackup, including copper thickness, dielectric thickness, and distance from the ground plane.

For this board, the calculated RF trace width was approximately **0.19 mm**.

This taught me that at high frequencies, a PCB trace is not simply a wire. Its physical geometry affects its electrical behavior.

### 4.4 USB Differential Pair Routing

USB D+ and D− are routed together as a differential pair.

The tutorial targets approximately **90 Ω differential impedance**.

Both the trace width and spacing between the two traces affect the final impedance.

The traces are kept together and follow similar paths so both signals experience approximately the same electrical environment.

### 4.5 Designing for the Manufacturer

The manufacturer has limits for things such as:

- minimum trace width
- minimum spacing
- drill size
- via size
- copper thickness
- layer stackup

The PCB should be designed around these manufacturing capabilities.

For controlled-impedance traces, the manufacturer should also confirm the final trace dimensions because they know the exact materials and stackup that will actually be fabricated.

### 4.6 ERC and DRC

I learned two important checks in KiCad.

**ERC — Electrical Rules Check** checks the schematic for electrical problems.

**DRC — Design Rules Check** checks the physical PCB for problems such as incorrect clearances, unconnected nets, and routing-rule violations.

These checks do not guarantee that the hardware will work, but they help catch many mistakes before manufacturing.

### 4.8 Manufacturing Files

The final KiCad project itself is not what the manufacturer directly uses.

The design is exported into files such as:

- Gerber files
- drill files
- Bill of Materials (BOM)
- component-position files
- manufacturing notes

The Gerbers describe the PCB layers, the drill files define holes and vias, the BOM identifies the components, and the component-position file tells the assembler where each component should be placed.

Manufacturing notes can also specify requirements such as the **50 Ω RF trace** and **90 Ω USB differential pair**.

## 5. Conclusion

For my first PCB project, the biggest thing I learned was that PCB design combines circuit design, component placement, power integrity, signal integrity, mechanical considerations, documentation, and manufacturing into one process.
